Connectors endpoint v2

Manage connectors — the source and destination integrations pipelines read from and write to.

Create a connector

POST /v2/connectors

Name Type Required Description
typestringYesOne of postgres, s3, snowflake, kafka, webhook.
directionstringYessource, destination, or bidirectional (webhook only).
configobjectYesType-specific connection details, e.g. connection string or IAM role ARN.
create-connector.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "type": "postgres",
    "direction": "source",
    "config": { "connection_string": "postgres://..." }
  }'

Rotate credentials

POST /v2/connectors/{id}/rotate — pauses every pipeline referencing this connector for the duration of the rotation, then resumes them automatically.

Shared connectors

A connector referenced by multiple pipelines is rotated once, for all of them. Check a connector's pipeline_count field before rotating during a busy window.

Health status

Quotas & billing v2

Godzilla enforces resource quotas per workspace according to your plan tier. This page details plan limits, quota dimensions, and the exact platform behavior when an account exceeds its quota.

1,000
requests / minute (Standard Tier)

Default API rate limit per workspace. Enterprise plans support customized limits up to 50,000+ req/min.

Plan tiers

Each workspace is subscribed to one of three tiers. Quotas apply across all pipelines, connectors, and API keys created within that workspace.

Plan Tier API Rate Limit Monthly Events Active Pipelines Connectors Support SLA
Developer 100 req/min 50,000 2 3 Community
Standard 1,000 req/min 5,000,000 25 20 1 business day
Enterprise Custom (10,000+) Custom / Unlimited Unlimited Unlimited 24/7 dedicated (1 hr SLA)

Quota dimensions

Godzilla accounts are governed by four primary quota dimensions:

  • API request rate: Per-minute sliding window limits on calls to https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2. See Limits, quotas & errors for header specifications.
  • Monthly event volume: The total number of events ingested, transformed, and delivered by your pipelines in a monthly billing cycle.
  • Active pipeline concurrency: The maximum number of pipelines running in active state simultaneously. Pipelines in draft or paused state do not count toward this limit.
  • Dead-letter queue retention: How long failed events remain available for inspection and replay (7 days on Developer, 30 days on Standard, 90 days on Enterprise).

What happens when you exceed your quota

Platform behavior depends on which quota dimension is exceeded and your workspace billing settings:

1. API rate limit exceeded

When API request volume exceeds the per-minute threshold, the gateway immediately rejects additional requests with HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests. Responses include a Retry-After header indicating the number of seconds until the rate limit resets.

429-rate-limit-response.json json 
{
  "error": {
    "code": "rate_limit_exceeded",
    "message": "API rate limit of 1000 req/min exceeded. Retry after 12 seconds.",
    "request_id": "req_rl_4901b"
  }
}

2. Monthly event quota exceeded

When event processing approaches or passes the monthly quota:

  • Warning notifications: Godzilla issues automated webhook notifications (account.quota_warning at 80% and account.quota_exceeded at 100%) and sends email alerts to workspace admins.
  • Standard tier (auto-overage enabled): Pipelines continue processing without interruption. Overage events are billed at $0.25 per 100,000 events on your monthly invoice.
  • Developer tier & hard caps: If auto-overage is disabled or you are on the Developer tier, pipelines transition to paused state. In-flight events finish processing, while new incoming events are buffered up to connector queue limits before upstream reads pause.
No event drops on overage

Godzilla never silently drops events when an account exceeds its quota. Events either flow with overage pricing or pause safely at the connector stage until the plan is upgraded or the billing cycle rolls over.

3. Pipeline or connector limits exceeded

Attempting to create a pipeline or connector beyond your plan limit via POST /v2/pipelines or POST /v2/connectors returns 403 Forbidden with error code quota_exceeded.

quota-exceeded-response.json json 
{
  "error": {
    "code": "quota_exceeded",
    "message": "Maximum active pipeline limit (25) reached for this workspace. Upgrade your plan to create more pipelines.",
    "request_id": "req_lim_9921c"
  }
}

Upgrading and billing management

You can upgrade your plan or configure overage settings at any time:

  • Self-serve upgrades: Upgrade from Developer to Standard instantly in the workspace dashboard under Settings > Billing.
  • Enterprise custom plans: For custom rate limits, VPC peering, and enterprise volume discounts, contact our sales team at sales@godzilladocs.dev or via Support / Contact.
Need help with rate limits or retries?

Read Limits, quotas & errors for HTTP response headers and error codes, or check the Handling errors & retries guide for automated backoff strategies.

Enterprise Custom (10,000+) Custom / Unlimited Unlimited Unlimited 24/7 dedicated (1 hr SLA)

Quota dimensions

Godzilla accounts are governed by four primary quota dimensions:

  • API request rate: Per-minute sliding window limits on calls to https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2. See Limits, quotas & errors for header specifications.
  • Monthly event volume: The total number of events ingested, transformed, and delivered by your pipelines in a monthly billing cycle.
  • Active pipeline concurrency: The maximum number of pipelines running in active state simultaneously. Pipelines in draft or paused state do not count toward this limit.
  • Dead-letter queue retention: How long failed events remain available for inspection and replay (7 days on Developer, 30 days on Standard, 90 days on Enterprise).

What happens when you exceed your quota

Platform behavior depends on which quota dimension is exceeded and your workspace billing settings:

1. API rate limit exceeded

When API request volume exceeds the per-minute threshold, the gateway immediately rejects additional requests with HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests. Responses include a Retry-After header indicating the number of seconds until the rate limit resets.

429-rate-limit-response.json json

  "error": {
    "code": "rate_limit_exceeded",
    "message": "API rate limit of 1000 req/min exceeded. Retry after 12 seconds.",
    "request_id": "req_rl_4901b"
  }
}

2. Monthly event quota exceeded

When event processing approaches or passes the monthly quota:

  • Warning notifications: Godzilla issues automated webhook notifications (account.quota_warning at 80% and account.quota_exceeded at 100%) and sends email alerts to workspace admins.
  • Standard tier (auto-overage enabled): Pipelines continue processing without interruption. Overage events are billed at $0.25 per 100,000 events on your monthly invoice.
  • Developer tier & hard caps: If auto-overage is disabled or you are on the Developer tier, pipelines transition to paused state. In-flight events finish processing, while new incoming events are buffered up to connector queue limits before upstream reads pause.
No event drops on overage

Godzilla never silently drops events when an account exceeds its quota. Events either flow with overage pricing or pause safely at the connector stage until the plan is upgraded or the billing cycle rolls over.

3. Pipeline or connector limits exceeded

Attempting to create a pipeline or connector beyond your plan limit via POST /v2/pipelines or POST /v2/connectors returns 403 Forbidden with error code quota_exceeded.

quota-exceeded-response.json json 
{
  "error": {
    "code": "quota_exceeded",
    "message": "Maximum active pipeline limit (25) reached for this workspace. Upgrade your plan to create more pipelines.",
    "request_id": "req_lim_9921c"
  }
}

Upgrading and billing management

You can upgrade your plan or configure overage settings at any time:

  • Self-serve upgrades: Upgrade from Developer to Standard instantly in the workspace dashboard under Settings > Billing.
  • Enterprise custom plans: For custom rate limits, VPC peering, and enterprise volume discounts, contact our sales team at sales@godzilladocs.dev or via Support / Contact.

Read Limits, quotas & errors for HTTP response headers and error codes, or check the Handling errors & retries guide for automated backoff strategies.

Transforms endpoint v2

Create and manage transform steps attached to pipelines. Transforms modify events in flight as they move from source to destination. See the Transforming events in flight guide for conceptual details and examples.

Create a transform step

POST /v2/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/transforms

Name Type Required Description
typestringYesOne of filter, reshape, or enrich.
conditionstringNoBoolean expression evaluated against incoming event (required for filter).
mappingobjectNoKey-value mapping of target field names to expressions (required for reshape).
fieldsobjectNoKey-value metadata dictionary to append to payload (required for enrich).
positionintegerNoZero-indexed execution order in pipeline. Defaults to appending at the end.
create-transform.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/pl_ingest_orders/transforms \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "type": "filter",
    "condition": "payload.status == '\''completed'\''"
  }'

List transform steps

GET /v2/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/transforms — returns the ordered list of transform steps configured on the pipeline.

transforms-list.json json 
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "tr_f18e9a2b",
      "type": "filter",
      "condition": "payload.status == 'completed'",
      "position": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "tr_r73c4d11",
      "type": "reshape",
      "mapping": {
        "order_id": "payload.id",
        "total_amount": "payload.amount_cents / 100"
      },
      "position": 1
    }
  ]
}

Transform types

Godzilla supports three transform types that can be chained together:

  • filter — evaluates a boolean condition; drops events that evaluate to false.
  • reshape — maps, renames, and calculates derived payload fields.
  • enrich — injects static metadata or dynamic platform values (e.g. $now).
In-flight execution

Adding or modifying transform steps creates a new version of the pipeline. Events currently in flight finish processing on the pipeline version they started on.

Webhooks endpoint v2

Subscribe to platform lifecycle events — such as pipeline.completed or connector.error — as outbound HTTP requests to a URL you control. This is the v2 replacement for v1's polling-only status checks; see the Migration guide if you're moving off v1.

Create a webhook subscription

POST /v2/webhooks

Name Type Required Description
typestringYesHTTPS endpoint Godzilla will POST events to.
eventsarrayYesList of event types to subscribe to, e.g. ["pipeline.failed"].
secretstringNoShared secret used to sign the X-Godzilla-Signature header. Auto-generated if omitted.
webhook-payload.json json 
{
  "id": "evt_wh_2091",
  "type": "pipeline.failed",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:14:02Z",
  "data": { "pipeline_id": "pl_ingest_orders", "error": "destination_timeout" }
}
Verify the signature

Always verify X-Godzilla-Signature before trusting a webhook payload. Unsigned or unverifiable requests to your endpoint should be rejected, not processed.

Delivery retries

A webhook delivery that doesn't receive a 2xx response is retried with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours, then marked failed. Failed deliveries are visible per-subscription and can be manually redelivered.

Connectors

A connector is a pre-built integration to an external system that a Pipeline reads from or writes to. Connectors handle authentication, batching, and retry behavior for a specific system so pipeline authors don't have to.

Connector direction

  • Source — emits events into a pipeline (e.g. a change-data-capture stream from Postgres).
  • Destination — receives events from a pipeline (e.g. writing rows into Snowflake).
  • Bidirectional — a small set of connectors, like the generic Webhook connector, can act as either.

Rotating connector credentials

Rotating a connector's credentials pauses any pipeline using it for the duration of the rotation. Plan credential rotations outside peak processing windows.

Connector health

Each connector reports a health status independent of any single pipeline: healthy, degraded, or down. A connector shared across multiple pipelines only needs to be fixed once — every pipeline referencing it recovers automatically.

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

event.json json 
{
  "id": "evt_8f2c1a90",
  "type": "order.created",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z",
  "source": "connector_postgres_orders",
  "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 }
}

Every event contains two distinct layers:

  • The envelope — top-level metadata managed by Godzilla (id, type, occurred_at, source).
  • The payload — the domain data object containing your application's fields and records.

Payload schemas and validation

While envelope metadata follows a fixed structure across Godzilla, the contents of the payload are governed by Schemas. Schemas declare the expected fields, data types, and value constraints for each event type.

Schemas

A schema defines the structural contract for an event's payload. While Godzilla enforces a standard top-level event envelope, schemas declare the exact data types, required properties, and value constraints of the user payload inside each event.

Declaring event payload shapes

Schemas in Godzilla use standard JSON Schema (draft-07) specifications. Each schema maps to an event type and declares what fields must be present and what data formats they must follow.

order-created.schema.json json 
{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "OrderCreatedPayload",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["order_id", "customer_id", "amount_cents", "currency"],
  "properties": {
    "order_id": {
      "type": "string",
      "pattern": "^ord_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$"
    },
    "customer_id": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "amount_cents": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 0
    },
    "currency": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["USD", "EUR", "GBP", "CAD"]
    },
    "metadata": {
      "type": "object"
    }
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Payload validation lifecycle

Validation runs automatically as data moves through a pipeline:

  1. Source ingestion: When a source connector emits an event, Godzilla matches the event's type against the registered schema and validates the payload.
  2. Transform boundaries: After each transform step that alters payload structures, the output can be re-validated before continuing down the pipeline.
  3. Destination write: Ensures only schema-compliant events reach destination sinks (such as Snowflake or PostgreSQL).
Validation occurs at runtime

Schema enforcement happens at event ingestion before expensive transforms or downstream writes occur. Malformed payloads are trapped early, protecting downstream systems from invalid state.

Validation modes

Pipelines can configure one of three validation modes depending on your data guarantees:

Mode Behavior on valid payload Behavior on invalid payload
strict Processed through pipeline Rejected immediately; event is moved to the dead-letter queue
permissive Processed through pipeline Processed with a validation_warning attribute attached and metric incremented
disabled Processed through pipeline Bypasses payload validation checks completely

Handling validation failures

When an event fails validation under strict mode, Godzilla emits a validation.failed error, cancels downstream processing for that event, and routes it to the pipeline's dead-letter queue. The dead-lettered record includes detailed validation diagnostics:

  • failing_path — the JSON pointer to the invalid field (e.g. /payload/amount_cents).
  • constraint — the rule that failed (e.g. minimum or required).
  • received_value — the actual invalid value received.

To inspect and replay failed events after correcting schema definitions or source data, see the Handling errors & retries guide and the Events replay endpoint.

Schema versioning and evolution

Event schemas evolve as your application grows. Godzilla supports backwards-compatible schema changes without downtime:

  • Additive changes: Adding optional fields or expanding enum values are non-breaking and can be deployed without updating existing event consumers.
  • Breaking changes: Adding required fields, removing fields, or changing data types require publishing a new schema version (e.g. order.created.v2) or applying a transform. See Transforming events in flight for reshaping payloads during migrations.

See also

  • Events — the envelope structure that wraps schema-validated payloads.
  • Pipelines — configuring validation modes and routing rules on pipelines.
  • Transforming events in flight — reshaping event payloads to match destination schemas.

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

schedule.json json 
{
  "schedule": "0 */4 * * *"
}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

Choosing between them

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries, or check out the Backfill historical data recipe.

Transforming events in flight

As events flow from a source connector to a destination connector, you can modify them in real time. This guide covers how to reshape payloads, filter out unwanted records, and enrich events with additional context inside a pipeline.

Configuring transforms

Transforms are defined as an ordered list in the transforms array of your pipeline definition. When creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint or managing individual steps with the Transforms endpoint, specify one or more transform steps.

pipeline-transforms.json json 
{
  "name": "orders-etl",
  "source_connector_id": "conn_pg_orders",
  "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_dw",
  "transforms": [
    {
      "type": "filter",
      "condition": "payload.status == 'completed'"
    },
    {
      "type": "reshape",
      "mapping": {
        "order_id": "payload.id",
        "total_amount": "payload.amount_cents / 100",
        "customer_email": "payload.email"
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "enrich",
      "fields": {
        "processed_at": "$now",
        "environment": "production"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Reshaping payloads

Use reshape transforms to map incoming fields to target schema structures, rename keys, calculate derived values, or drop unnecessary nested data before writing to the destination.

OperationExample mapping
Field renaming{ "user_id": "payload.account_id" }
Calculations{ "amount_usd": "payload.amount_cents / 100" }
Flattening nested fields{ "city": "payload.address.city" }

Filtering events

Filter steps evaluate a boolean condition against each event. Events that evaluate to true proceed to the next step, while events evaluating to false are dropped cleanly without triggering an error or alerting the dead-letter queue.

Filter early for performance

Place filter steps at the beginning of the transforms list to avoid executing unnecessary reshape or enrichment steps on records that will ultimately be discarded.

Enriching events

Enrichment steps append new metadata or computed context to the event payload. Common enrichments include injecting processing timestamps ($now), platform metadata, or static environment tags needed by downstream analytics systems.

Error handling in transforms

If an event encounters an unhandled evaluation error during a transform step (such as a type mismatch or missing required field), it is retried according to the pipeline's retry policy before being sent to the dead-letter queue. See Handling errors & retries for details on debugging and replaying failed transforms.

Next steps

Learn how to handle unexpected failures and replay dead-lettered events in Handling errors & retries, see Scheduling & triggers to control how your pipeline runs, or follow the Fan-out to multiple destinations recipe for routing different transforms to separate systems.

v1 returned bare error strings. v2 wraps every error in an object with a stable code field. Update any error handling that matched on message text — see the error shape reference.

v1 is retired

Backfill historical data

When connecting a new destination or onboarding a new dataset, you often need to ingest historical records in addition to streaming new changes. This recipe demonstrates how to run large-scale historical backfills through a pipeline safely without exhausting rate limits or blocking live events.

Prerequisites

Ensure your source and destination connectors are active and verified. See Connecting a data source for setup details.

Architecture overview

Rather than modifying your live streaming pipeline, create a dedicated backfill pipeline with bounded source offsets. This provides two key benefits:

  • Workload isolation: High-throughput backfill traffic does not starve or add latency to real-time events.
  • Custom rate limits: You can tune concurrency, batch sizes, and retry backoffs specifically for bulk loading.

1. Create a dedicated backfill pipeline

Use the Pipelines endpoint to create a pipeline configured with bounded timestamps or query constraints on the source connector.

create-backfill-pipeline.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "backfill-orders-2025",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_pg_orders",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_dw",
    "config": {
      "mode": "backfill",
      "start_timestamp": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
      "end_timestamp": "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z",
      "batch_size": 5000,
      "max_concurrency": 4
    }
  }'

2. Configure transform rules for bulk ingestion

Bulk backfills may contain legacy data formats or outdated schema versions. Attach schema normalization transforms to map older records into your current target format.

backfill-transforms.json json 
{
  "transforms": [
    {
      "type": "enrich",
      "fields": {
        "is_backfill": true,
        "backfilled_at": "$now"
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "reshape",
      "mapping": {
        "id": "payload.order_id",
        "amount": "payload.total_price",
        "created_at": "payload.created_at"
      }
    }
  ]
}

3. Managing destination rate limits and quotas

Backfills push high volumes of data in short periods. Avoid throttling destination systems by adjusting concurrency settings and observing platform quotas.

Throttle to protect downstream systems

If your destination database or API enforces strict write quotas, set max_concurrency low and monitor Limits, quotas & errors to prevent cascading 429 status codes.

4. Monitoring and verifying completion

Track progress by checking pipeline metrics or subscribing to platform lifecycle events. When all historical records have been processed, the backfill pipeline status transitions to completed.

check-status.sh bash 
curl https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/pipe_backfill_2025/stats \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"

If any individual records fail, inspect the dead-letter queue and replay failed records as described in Handling errors & retries.

Next steps

Once your backfill completes, explore the Fan-out to multiple destinations recipe to route your streaming data to multiple downstream storage systems simultaneously.

import { Godzilla } from "@godzilla/sdk";

Create a pipeline

Maps directly onto the Pipelines endpoint — see the Building your first pipeline guide for the concepts.

const pipeline = await godzilla.pipelines.create({
  name: "ingest-orders",
  sourceConnectorId: "conn_pg_orders",
  destinationConnectorId: "conn_snowflake_dw",
});

Listening for webhooks

import { verifyWebhookSignature } from "@godzilla/sdk";

const isValid = verifyWebhookSignature(rawBody, signatureHeader, webhookSecret);

Security & compliance overview

How Godzilla protects data moving through your pipelines.

Encryption

All API traffic requires TLS 1.2+. Connector credentials are encrypted at rest and are never returned in full by any endpoint after creation.

Credential handling

See Authentication for API key handling, and Connectors endpoint for connector credential rotation.

Least privilege

We recommend scoping every source connector's credentials to read-only access, as described in the Connecting a data source guide.

Data residency

Events are processed in the region your workspace was created in and are not replicated across regions by default.

Reporting a vulnerability

Contact the team through Support / Contact — do not file security reports as public issues.

Troubleshooting / FAQ

Common problems, and where in the docs to go for the full explanation.

My pipeline isn't processing events

Check the source connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint. A down connector stalls every pipeline that reads from it. If it's healthy, confirm the pipeline itself is active and not paused — see Scheduling & triggers.

Events keep failing and landing in the dead-letter queue

Walk through Handling errors & retries — it covers both diagnosing the failure and replaying events once fixed.

I'm not receiving webhook deliveries

Verify your endpoint returns a 2xx status and that you're checking X-Godzilla-Signature correctly — a rejected signature looks identical to a dropped delivery from the outside. Full details in the Webhooks endpoint reference.

I'm getting 429s

You've hit the standard-tier limit described in Limits, quotas & errors. Back off using the Retry-After header, or review Quotas & billing if your workload needs higher plan tier limits or customized throughput.

Migrating from v1?

A number of "it worked yesterday" reports trace back to v1's offset pagination or polling patterns carried over into v2 code. See the Migration guide.

Still stuck?

Reach the team via Support / Contact.
